headline: Records keep climbing even as the long bond sends a warning
body: Equities extended their run again Tuesday: the S&P 500 pushed to roughly 7,782 and the Nasdaq closed at a fresh record, with megacap tech doing the heavy lifting -- Nvidia up over 2%, Tesla up a similar amount, and Microsoft adding 1.5%. A seven-plus percent pop in SpaceX-related shares on pipeline-expansion news added to the single-stock excitement. The broader tailwind is a familiar one: fading expectations that the Fed needs to stay restrictive, a pullback in crude that has taken some geopolitical risk premium out of the tape, and analysts marking up earnings-growth estimates toward the high-20s percent range for the coming season. Congress clearing its funding deadline without a shutdown has also removed a headline risk that had been nagging markets for weeks.

The friction sits further out on the curve rather than in equities themselves: the 10-year Treasury yield pushed back above 5.3% and the 30-year breached 5.7%, levels not seen in roughly 24 years, even as stocks kept grinding to new highs. That split -- risk assets celebrating while long-term borrowing costs climb to multi-decade peaks -- is the kind of divergence that tends to get reconciled eventually, one way or the other. Retail chatter today leaned more on idiosyncratic drama (viral loss and margin-call stories circulating on trading forums) than on any coherent macro call, so this read leans primarily on price action and the yield move rather than social sentiment. Net effect: a market that looks confidently greedy on the surface but is quietly digesting a much higher cost of long-term capital underneath.
